title: The barren fig tree and the two sons (Matthew 21:18–32)
word: The barren fig tree and the two sons
hookLine: a tree with leaves and no fruit, and a son who said no and went
tomorrow: what happens to the stone the builders threw away?
last: OUT OF THE MOUTHS OF BABES.

lines: I GO, SIR, AND WENT NOT.
cards: "On my way!" says the text, sent from the couch. A small, friendly, familiar fib. Jesus tells a story about exactly that, and it answers yesterday's question.

"A certain man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard. He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went." The father asks the second son.
He says, "I go, sir: and went not." Which one did the will of his father? Even the people questioning Jesus answer: the first.

teach.b: The story sits next to a stranger one. That morning, hungry, Jesus finds a fig tree by the road with nothing on it but leaves, and it "withered away." The disciples marvel, and he doesn't explain the tree.
He turns it into a word about prayer instead. Some readers hear the tree as a picture of anything that looks alive and gives nothing: all leaf, no fruit. Matthew leaves that reading to us.
Then the sting of the two sons.

Jesus tells his questioners that tax collectors and prostitutes are going into the kingdom ahead of them, because those people believed John the Baptist, and his listeners didn't change their minds even after seeing it.
Notice who comes out well. Not the polite son.

teach.h: IT CARES WHERE HIS FEET WENT.
teach.b: The one who said no, and then went.
The story doesn't pretend his first answer was fine. It cares where his feet ended up.

how: Christians use the word repent for a change of mind that shows up in what a person does, and some preachers use this parable to explain it.

games.q: what does “the barren fig tree and the two sons” mean?
o: leaves without fruit, and a no that became a yes
a warning about planting trees on holy ground
a harvest feast where two brothers share figs

games.q: two sons and a tree — tap the pairs.
p: I go, sir, and went not

s: Jesus praises the son who answered politely
the polite son said I go, sir, and went not. the one who said no and then went did the will.
Jesus' questioners themselves answer that the first son did the father's will
they say, the first; then Jesus turns the story on them.
Matthew explains what the withered fig tree stands for
he turns it into a word about prayer and leaves the tree unexplained.

games.q: a club at your school posts every week about its food drive, but hasn't collected anything in months. which picture from Matthew 21 do some readers see in that?
o: the fig tree: all leaf, no fruit.
the first son, who said I will not.
games.why: Matthew doesn't explain the tree; some readers hear it as anything that looks alive and gives nothing. all leaf, no fruit.

practice: Stand up, if you can, and feel your weight settle into your feet: heels, the balls of your feet, your toes. Bring to mind one thing you said no to that you'd now like to do.
Then take a few slow steps across the room, toward the door, feeling each foot land, and let that walk be the son's afterward: he repented, and went.
If standing isn't possible right now, press your feet into the floor and feel them carry the same decision.

wordCard.voice: The barren fig tree and the two sons. Leaves without fruit, and a yes without going, set side by side.

orig.note: Greek: to regret, to change one's mind; behind 'he repented' in Matthew 21:29.

carryVoice: Your line: he repented and went. A late yes still walks to the vineyard. Until tomorrow.
